Applying the principles that emerges from the reading of the Supreme Court and High Court judgments, it can be concluded that comprehensive 'CCTV based City Surveillance System' can be termed as immovable property for following reasons:

(1)

CCTV based Surveillance System have permanently been fastened to the things attached to the earth.

(2)

The CCTV based Surveillance System cannot not be shifted without first dismantling it and then erecting it at another site. In view of above facts and having regard to the principles laid down in the judgments of the High Courts and Supreme Court, it is firmly viewed that set up of a comprehensive CCTV based city surveillance system for the city of Pune and Pimpri-Chinchwad does result into installation/commissioning of immovable property wherein transfer of property in goods is involved in the execution of the contract and thus the 'Surveillance Project' is a works contract as defined in sub-section 119 of section 2 and is supply of services as per 6(a) of Schedule II of the GST Act. And therefore the amount received for the supply of services post-GST are taxable under the provision of GST Act.

What is rate of tax applicable on supply of works contract services by applicant under GST Act ?

A conclusion has been drawn that the applicant is supplying works contract services, The Notification No.11/2017 Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 is applicable to the instant case. As per the said Notification it is very clear that the composite supply of works contract as in the subject case falls under (ii) attracting 18 per cent GST. The said Notification was amended on 22-8-2017 vide Notification No. 20/2017 Central Tax (Rate). As per the said Notification with the amendment also it is very clear that the composite supply of works contract as in the subject case falls under (ii) attracting 18 per cent GST. The said Notification 11/2017 was further amended on 21-9-2017 vide Notification No. 24/2017 Central Tax (Rate). Even with the amendment the applicant's position has not changed. Their composite supply of works contract as in the subject case falls under (ii) attracting 18 per cent GST. The said Notification 11/2017 was also further amended on 25-1-2018 vide Notification No. 01/2018 Central Tax (Rate). Even with the amendment aforesaid the applicant's position has remained unchange The Surveillance project remains works contract as in the subject case falls under (ii) attracting GST at rate of 18 per cent. However in the subject it is seen that applicant is providing composite supply of works contract in respect of surveillance project to Government of Maharashtra but the reduced rate of tax is available only if the work is of the type of original work. The expression 'Original work' has not been defined under any of the Notifications applicable to the present case. The expression 'original work' has assigned meaning under the CPWD Works Manual 2014. It means:

(i)

all new constructions,

(ii)

all types of additions, alterations and/or special repairs to newly acquired assets, abandoned

Or

damaged assets that are required to make them workable.

(iii)

major replacements or remodelling of a portion of an existing structure or installation or other works, which results in a genuine increase in the life and value of the property.

Thus' Original Works' would mean; all new constructions; all types of additions and alterations to abandoned or damaged structures on land that are required to make them workable; erection, installation etc. that results in increase in life and value of property. In the instant case the work done by the applicant does not appear to be original works.

Hence from the above discussions it is found that in the instant case, the contract is not related to any original work and is in the nature of composite supply of Works Contract. Hence, it is held that the activity of the applicant in the instant case is nothing but a composite supply of Works Contract, not being original works and they will be covered under Sr. No. 3, item No. (ii) of Notification No. 11/2017 dated 28-6-2017 as amended by Notification No. 1/2018 dated 25-1-2018 and attract 18 per cent GST (9 per cent each of CGST and SGST). [Para 5]

AAR by order held that where Government of India, Ministry of Human Resource Development is exercising full control over activities of IITs all over country, IIT, Bhubaneswar qualifies to be called and termed as a 'Government Entity' for purpose of GST law, however mere fact that number of works are entrusted by IIT Bhubaneswar to applicant under a single contract/agreement, would not make it entitled to be categorised as 'composite supply', and, thus, entire work under said contract shall not be entitled to concessional rate in terms of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

On appeal:

In the application itself it is stated that MPPGCL has been established by the Government of Madhya Pradesh and the Government of Madhya Pradesh has a 100 per cent shareholding in the company and is also exercising full control over the activities of the said company. Thus, MPPGCL qualifies to be called and termed as a 'Government Entity' for the purpose of GST law, as it fulfils the necessary and sufficient conditions laid down under notification No. 11/2017. [Para 5.4]

Now, the said Government Entity i.e. MPPGCL has been entrusted with the work of power generation in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The essential and sole work entrusted to MPPGCL by the Government of Madhya Pradesh is of electricity (power) generation. MPPGCL has awarded a works contract for construction of 599 residential quarters to the applicant. However, the civil construction of residential quarters is neither the primary work entrusted to MPPGCL nor it has any bearing on the work i.e. power generation by any means. Thus, the benefit of concessional rate of 12 per cent GST should not be available to this particular works contract awarded to the applicant. The intention of the legislature has been to give concessional rate to such work which has been entrusted to a Government entity for public interest in general. Any work having direct involvement in the entrusted work i.e. power generation would merit exemption envisaged under Sr.No.3(vi)(c) of the Notification No.11/2017-CT (Rate) under CGST Act and corresponding notification under MPGST Act 2017, but extrapolating and extending this concessional rate to any or all activities of MPPGCL will not only be unwarranted but also defeat the very purpose of concessional rate. [Para 5.5]

The activity in question definitely did not have any relation to the principal work of power generation entrusted by the State Government to MPPGCL, and, thus, the works contract service of construction of residential quarters would attract GST at the rate of 18 per cent (9 per cent CGST + 9 per cent SGST) in terms of Notification No.11/2017-CT Rate dated 28-6-2017 and corresponding notification under MPGST Act, 2017. [Para 5.6]

Thus, the impugned activity of the applicant would attract GST at the rate of 18 per cent (9 per cent CGST + 9 per cent SGST) classifiable under SAC 9954 read with Notification No.11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) and corresponding notification under MPGST Act 2017. [Para 5.7]

Facts in the case of Harekrishna Developers, In re [2008] 14 STT 175 (AAR - New Delhi) 3.2 The applicant-firm intends to develop on its own plot of land a residential complex having more than twelve residential units with a club house and other common facilities. It will sell plots of land inside the complex to prospective buyers who will enter into a works contract with the applicant for the construction of residential units. The applicant itself will execute a part of the works contract [‘activity No. 3’] and for remaining part, the applicant will further enter into a works contract with other contractors [‘activity No. 4’]. However, goods for construction will be purchased/acquired by the applicant and the property in those goods will be transferred to buyers of the housing units and such transfer would be exigible to tax as sale of goods. The applicant sought advance ruling of the Authority on questions of its liability in these two types of activities, and also on question of rate of tax in case of activity No. 3.

The applicant contends that since the works contract in activities 3 and 4 involves construction of a new building-such an activity can only be covered under(ii)( b) in the Explanation to section 65(105)(zzzza). Since the new building proposed to be constructed in the course of the execution of the works contract is a residential one, and is not for the purpose of commerce or industry, such a works contract will not fall under (b) and therefore, will not attract service tax. The applicant further states that a works contract for construction of a new building for residential purposes is also not covered under any of the remaining classifications in (ii) of the Explanation to clause (zzzza). The classification (c) which covers ‘construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof’ is not applicable in applicant’s case as the works contract is for construction of an individual residential unit and not for construction of a residential complex.

Decision in the case of Harekrishna Developers (supra )

3.3 Authority for Advance Ruling held:

1. To attract service tax under sub-clause (zzzza) of section 65(105), a works contract has to meet the two conditions: (i) and (ii) in the Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). The facts narrated by the applicant indicated that condition (i) is met in the instant case as the transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract is exigible to tax as sale of goods under the local Sales Tax Act. To meet condition (ii), the activity involved in the works contract in activity Nos. 3 and 4 has to be covered by at least one of the classifications (a ) to (e) in the Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). Proceeding serially, one finds that building of a residential house on a sub-plot in a residential complex is clearly not covered in (a). As pointed out by the applicant itself, it is also not covered by (b) which covers construction of a new building intended primarily for commerce and industry and does not cover construction of a new building. Item (c) of sub-clause (zzzza) of clause (105) covers ‘construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof’.

2. As per the draft of the works contract submitted, it is clear that such contracts will be for construction of individual houses on sub-plots located within the plot owned by the applicant on which the applicant proposes to develop a residential housing project. As per the applicant’s own narration, the residential project to be constructed on this plot would have at least 12 residential units, a club house and other common facilities and the layout of the project would be approved by the prescribed authority under the relevant law in force. Such a project constructed as per activity Nos. 3 and 4 squarely conforms to the definition of a ‘residential complex’ given in clause (91a) of section 65, and the individual houses constructed get covered under the definition of a ‘residential unit’ contained therein. Execution of the works contract, thus, involves construction of a part of a new ‘residential complex’ and is covered by (c).

CONSTRUCTION NOT IN RESPECT OF RAILWAYS - TAXABLE

1. Our company has executed works contract for Central Rail Side Warehousing Corporation Ltd. (CRWC) at Ranchi (Jharkhand). The nature of works is construction, erection and installation of PEB structures of steel and incidental works for warehouse complex. The period of contract executed is 1st April, 2007 to 31st March, 2012. The service tax department is asking for payment of service tax for the contract value of this work of say Rs. 1 crore.

We understand that Railways is exempted from service tax. The definition of railways as given in the Railways Act includes its warehouses. So, our company should not be liable to service tax on such works contract of construction, erection and installation of warehouses. Use of the warehouses is not exempted but construction of railway warehouses is exempted.

Constitution of CRWC is as follows: Indian Railways have entered into a MOU with the Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) as its strategic partner for development of integrated railside warehouse complexes. CWC has created a SPV as its subsidiary, named as CRWC with the sole purpose of developing railside warehousing complexes (not other complexes). The Indian Railways has provided land near various railway terminals and the CRWC has constructed and erected railway warehousing complexes on the land by contracting with our company. Indian Railway will get its share of profit by way of profit sharing from CRWC.

Kindly enlighten us whether the stand of the company is correct that construction of railside warehousing by Indian Railways in partnership with CRWC should not be taxable.

Railway is defined in section 2(31) of the Railways Act, 1989; the same is reproduced below -

"railway" means a railway, or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods, and includes-

"(a)

all lands within the fences or other boundary marks indicating the limits of the land appurtenant to a railway;

(b)

all lines of rails, sidings, or yards, or branches used for the purposes of, or in connection with, a railway;

(c)

all electric traction equipments, power supply and distribution installations used for the purposes of, or in connection with, a railway;

(d)

all rolling stock, stations, officers warehouses, wharves, workshops, factories, fixed plant and machinery, roads and streets, running rooms, rest houses, institutes, hospitals, water works and water supply installations, staff dwellings and any other works constructed for the purpose of, or in connection with, railway;

(e)

all vehicles which are used on any road for the purposes of traffic of a railway and owned, hired or worked by a railway; and

(f)

all ferries, ships, boats and rafts which are used on any canal, river, lake or other navigable inland waters for the purposes of the traffic of a railway and owned, hired or worked by a railway administration,

but does not include-

(i)

a tramway wholly within a municipal area; and

(ii)

lines of rails built in any exhibition ground, fair, park or any other place solely for the purpose of recreation.

The relevant taxable services, viz., Commercial construction services and works contract services exclude services/works contracts in respect of roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams.

The query can be answer solely on basis of clause (d) of the definition, as it lists various places to be considered as 'railways'.

Services provided by railway include transport of passengers and goods and, constructions necessary therefor are covered by the term 'railways'. The words "officers warehouses"... "rest houses"... "any other works" … "for the purpose of railways" or "in connection with railways" are wide enough to cover warehouses meant for storage of goods transported by the railways.

If that is the case, the services will be considered as having been provided in respect of construction of warehouse for use of the railways.

However, construction of warehouses meant for commercial use by railways and not for use of railways will not be covered under 'railways' and services provided would be not considered as 'in respect of' railways.

Please note that the services must be provided "in respect of" railways and not merely "to" railways.

Hence, it appears that the services provided by your client would be liable to service tax.

Illustration 2 - M/s. XYZ Ltd. are engaged in carrying out works contract liable to VAT under the State-VAT laws. They had started a works contract on 1-6-2012 and had opted for composition scheme for payment of VAT and service tax both. On 1-7-2012, since the composition scheme stands withdrawn, their works contract (not being original works) falls under rule 2A(ii)(C) of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006 (value cannot be determined on actual basis under Rule 2A(i) ibid). How should they determine their liability to pay service tax in respect of the said works contract in the following situations -

(i) service provided, bills raised and amounts received prior to 1-7-2012 ;

(ii) service provided and bill raised prior to 1-7-2012, but, amounts received on or after 1-7-2012 ;

(iii) service provided prior to 1-7-2012, but bill raised and amount received on or after 1-7-2012 ;

(iv) service provided, bill raised and amounts received on or after 1-7-2012.

Solution - Works Contract Service is notified as continuous supply of service for which Point of Taxation is determinable under rule 3 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011. However, in case of change in effective rate of tax, rule 4 ibid shall apply, as rule 4 ibid has overriding effect.

Under composition scheme, M/s. XYZ Ltd. was liable to pay service tax @ 4.8% of total amount charged, while, w.e.f. 1-7-2012, the effective rate of service tax shall be @ 7.2% of total amount charged (12% of 60% of total amount). This is a case of change in effective rate of tax for which the Point of Taxation shall be determined under rule 4 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011.

Accordingly, -

(i) service provided, bills raised and amounts received prior to 1-7-2012 - Point of taxation shall be prior to 1-7-2012 and composition rate 4.8% will apply ;

(ii) service provided and bill raised prior to 1-7-2012, but, amounts received on or after 1-7-2012 - Point of taxation shall be the date of invoice i.e., prior to 1-7-2012 and composition rate 4.8% will apply - Rule 4(a)(ii) of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011.

(iii) service provided prior to 1-7-2012, but bill raised and amount received on or after 1-7-2012 - The point of taxation shall be date of payment or issuing of invoice, whichever is earlier i.e., on or after 1-7-2012 and new valuation under rule 2(ii)(C) and effective rate of 7.2% shall apply - rule 4(a)(i) of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011.

(iv) service provided, bill raised and amounts received on or after 1-7-2012 - Point of taxation shall be on or after 1-7-2012 and new valuation under Rule 2(ii)(C) and effective rate of 7.2% shall apply.

8. Section 7 CGST defines supply in an inclusive manner meaning it is a widened and broadened connotation. Essentially, a flat under construction and intended to be sold to a buyer is sale of immovable property, but when it is undergoing construction there is an element of service and consequently, it was necessary to treat construction of flats as a supply of service vide Section 7(1)(d) read with item no 5(b) of Schedule II. 9. Schedule of Goods and Service Tax rates for services approved by GST Council laying down fitment of rates of services states at entry 19 that "Construction of a complex, civil structure or part thereof intended for sale to a buyer wholly or partly" will bear GST at 12.5% with full input tax credit, but no refund of overflow of input tax credit. The entry also explains that the value of land is included in the amount charged from the service recipient. Simultaneously, rate of GST for composite works contract as defined in Section 2(119) vide entry 27 is 18% with full input tax credit. In substance and effect, though construction of flat is treated as a service yet it is akin to a works contract. Drawing such a cue implies that concession of 6% is given to factor in value of land thereby leading to a calculation of 33% of abatement on the total consideration. However, prescription of such a standard rate of abatement [assumed] does not take into realities of cheap, medium, semi-luxury, luxurious and elite segments where composition of land value would considerably vary. Moreover, in semi-rural developing towns, presumed rate of 33% in respect of land value may be on higher side leading to excess input credit over 12% output tax inasmuch as input supplies for builders mostly carry a rate of 18% to 28% which as per schedule of rates as seen above is not refundable. In cases, where input tax credit falls short of GST rate of 12% profits of builders will truncate or lead passing of burden on to consumers. In my opinion, this matters ought to have been formulated by the legislature in a flexible manner through a methodology by way of rules to reckon local factors.

10. Another daunting controversy that may arise is whether the overflow of input tax credit is to be worked per project or on a net basis for all projects put together. Section 16 of CGST provides that every person shall subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed and in the manner specified in Section 49 be entitled to the credit of any input tax in respect of any supply of goods and services or both to him which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of his business and the amount shall be credited to the electronic ledger of such person. In my opinion, looking at the wording of Section 16 aforesaid read with Section 17 better view appears to be that an overall picture of all projects will have to be undertaken and not project wise. No guidance is found either in the Act or the relevant rules as what are the implications of GST in a case when a project undertaken by the builder where he has to give flats to the owner of land in discharge of consideration for obtaining development rights. Assuming in a particular case, the developers have to provide 100 flats to owners and there other 200 flats for free sale; in former case he will be a contractor levying GST at 18% with input tax credit, whereas in the latter case, the rate would be 12% with full input tax credit but no refund of overflow credit in a situation where flats are sold before they are fully developed. In the aforementioned example, there can controversy as to how the overflow of input tax credit to be computed being the difference between the rate of GST on input supplies and 18% GST rate more particularly, after considering common input supplies and capital goods employed for both types of flats. Moreover, disputes will arise as to what is time of supply of the 100 units to be allotted to owners more specifically, if land is not parted physically at one go, but in stages. Can we say the supply of flats is complete when possession of land is given despite the fact that flats are yet to be constructed? If the free sale flats are sold in stages question will emanate as to whether input tax credit is to be accumulated or can be claimed while construction is progressing without any sale? It would be best to issue clarifications on these and other potential roadblocks that may lead to avoidable litigation.

DELHI METRO RAIL CORPORATION IS NOT 'RAILWAYS' 2. Our company has executed works contract for the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) by way of supply and erection of PEB structures for six elevated stations of DMRC in New Delhi during 1st April, 2008 to 31st March, 2010. The value of the contract is say of Rs. 1 crore. The service tax department is asking for payment of service tax on works executed for DMRC. The company is of the view that DMRC is railways, and the works executed for railway is exempted in service tax. But the service tax department says that DMRC is not included in railways, as it is a separate corporation from the Indian Railways. We understand that the definition of 'railways' as per the Railways Act is not restricted to the Indian railways. It says "Railways means a railway or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods." Thus, whether it is DMRC or Indian Railways, both are railways and works contract executed to any of them is exempted.

You may kindly enlighten us whether the stand of the company is right that the works contract of supply and erection of PEB structures for six elevated stations of DMRC is exempted.

As per section 2(31) of the Railways Act, 1989, "railway" means a railway, or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods. It doesn't include a tramway wholly within a Municipal area.

The relevant taxable services, viz., commercial construction services and works contract services exclude services/works contract in respect of roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams.

As per clause (20) of section 2 the aforesaid Act :

(20) "Government railway" means a railway owned by the Central Government;

As per clause (g) ibid :

(g) "railway administration", in relation to-

(a)

a Government railway, means the General Manager of a Zonal Railway; and

(b)

a non-Government railway person means the person who is the owner or lessee of the railway or the person working for the railway under an agreement;

As per the meaning given to it "railway" means a railway, or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods. Thus, railways may be Government owned or private owned. Even private-owned railways is railways within the meaning of the Act. However, a 'tramway' is excluded.

Further, present section 66D(o) provides that service of transportation of passengers, with or without accompanied belongings, by-

(i)

a stage carriage;

(ii)

railways in a class other than-

(A)

first class; or

(B)

an air-conditioned coach;

(iii)

metro, monorail or tramway;...

shall be in the negative list.

Thus, the present law conceives of 'railways' differently from 'metro or monorail or tramway'.

As per Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia, a tram-train is a light-rail public transport system where trams run through from an urban tramway network to main-line railway lines which are shared with conventional trains. This combines the tram's flexibility and accessibility with a train's greater speed, and bridges the distance between a main railway station and a city centre. There is also a train-tram, which is a train modified to run also on tramlines. Generally, the tram-train and train-tram are interchangeable, although a train-tram is based on a train design modified to also run as a tram and a tram-train is based on a tram design modified also to run on a train line.

Hence, it appears that Delhi Metro is a 'tramway' and not a 'railway'. The services may not be eligible for exemption.

[A useful reference may also be made to : http://www.hindustantimes.com/India-news/Mumbai/Mumbai-Metro-Is-it-a-tramway-or-a-railway/Article1-763834.aspx]

However, in Bangalore Metro Rail Corpn. Ltd. v. Ministry of Finance [2013] 39 STT 107/31 taxmann.com 381 (Kar.), the Court has ruled that services provided in relation to execution of works contract for Metro Rail Corporation would not be liable to service tax, in view of provisions of section 65(105)(zzzza), excluding services provided in relation to railways.

There is no doubt that the project undertaken by the applicant pertains to an affordable housing project. In the subject project, the applicant will be constructing dwelling units of less than 60 sq. mtrs. carpet area as well as dwelling units having carpet area greater than 60 sq. mtrs. [Para 5.14.1] It is found that common amenities form part of the overall construction service and are always naturally bundled when offered to the customer. Therefore, such services will qualify as composite supply of works contract service, where the principal supply would be, construction services. Accordingly, the rate applicable to the principal supply will also be applicable to common amenities. The word 'housing project' cannot be confined only to dwelling units, it would also include within its fold, other common amenities, structures, etc. Common amenities form part of the overall construction service and are always naturally bundled when offered to the customer. Therefore, such services will qualify as composite supply of works contract service wherein provision of construction services is the principal supply. Accordingly, the rate applicable to the principal supply will also be applicable to common amenities i.e. in respect of dwelling units having area less than 60 sq. mtrs., the GST rate would be 12 per cent and in cases of dwelling units having area greater than 60 sq. mtrs. the GST rate would be 18 per cent. [Para 5.14.2]

It is held that the applicant's case is covered under the concessional rate of 12 per cent (8 per cent GST after deducting value of land), under Heading 9954 (Construction Services), (v)(da) of above mentioned Notification No. 11/2017, as amended since the project undertaken by them falls under the definition of 'Affordable Housing'. The benefit of reduced rate would be available to them only in the cases of supply effected after 25-1-2018 i.e., the date on which Notification No. 1/2018-Central Tax (Rate) was issued and the benefit of this reduced rate would be applicable only in case of amenities pertaining to only those flats which are of carpet area upto 60 sq. mtrs. In case of amenities provided to purchasers of flats which have carpet area more than 60 sq. mtrs., the applicant would be required to pay GST at normal applicable rate i.e. at the rate of 18 per cent GST. [Para 5.14]

Subject project consists of both, dwelling units less than and also greater than 60 sq. mtrs. Benefit of concessional rate is only available to 'Affordable Housing' as already discussed above. The definition of 'Affordable Housing' is confined to dwelling units with carpet area of not more than 60 square meters. Thus, concessional rate available to applicant is only in respect of low cost houses along with amenities constructed by the applicant. The common amenities and areas are a part of 'Affordable Housing Project' and therefore the applicant will be entitled to benefit of concessional rate for the same, only when they are a part of low cost houses, i.e. units less than 60 sq. mtrs. The applicant will thus have to discharge GST at the rate of 12 per cent (after deducting value of land) on works contract services provided for the construction of the units and common areas and amenities, which do qualify the criteria of low cost houses. Since concessional rate would be available only for construction services pertaining to dwelling units less than 60 sq. mtrs. Including common areas and amenities on pro rata basis, construction services including common areas and amenities on pro rata basis, performed by the applicant in respect of dwelling units exceeding 60 sq. mtrs. would be liable to full rate of GST, i.e., 18 per cent. Hence the applicant is supplying works contract services. It is also apparent that the nature of the works undertaken by the applicant is not in the nature of 'original works'.

The second question raised by the applicant is whether these contracts can be classified as works contracts as per GST law and whether Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended by Notification No. 01/2018 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018 is applicable to the instant case.

As per the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, it is very clear that the composite supply of works contract as in the subject case falls under Sr. No. 3, Item (ii) of the said Notification attracting 18 per cent GST. The said Notification was amended from time to time vide Notification No. 20/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 22-8-2017, Notification No. 24/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 21-9-2017, Notification No. 31/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 13-10-2017 and Notification No. 46/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 11-11-2017.

The aforesaid Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 11-11-2017 was also further amended on 25-1-2018 vide Notification No. 1/2018 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018 and vide this amendment item (v) was changed to include composite supply of works contract as defined in clause (119) of section 2 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, supplied by way of construction, …………..pertaining to, (a) railways, including monorail and metro.

In the instant case, it is seen that the applicant is providing composite supply of works contract in respect of Metro but the reduced rate of tax is available only if the work is of the type of original works.

Original works would mean all new constructions; all types of additions and alterations to abandoned or damaged structures on land that are required to make them workable; erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery or equipment or structures, whether pre-fabricated or otherwise, etc. In the instant case, the work done by the applicant does not appear to be original works. The applicant itself has stated that here it would like to draw your attention to the fact that the scope of work does not include construction of entire project of metro stations, railway line, power supply, civil structures, etc. but scope include Shifting LT, HT Overhead lines crossing which are obstructing metro railway path and providing LT, HT underground cables for Nagpur Metro Rail Project. The work is not construction of metro rail project but this is shifting of existing utilities obstructing metro railway path and providing supplying and installation of new underground cable along with its accessories.

In view of the aforesaid, it is seen that in the instant case the contract is not related to any original work and is in the nature of composite supply of works contract. Hence the activity of the applicant is nothing but a composite supply of works contract, not being original works and they will be covered under Sr. No. 3, item (ii) of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended by Notification No. 1/2018 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018 and attract 18 per cent GST (9 per cent each of CGST and Maharashtra GST). To transfer the existing credits in the GST regime, condition has been kept that such credit must have been admissible in the GST regime. Therefore, builders should be able to transfer the following credits to the GST regime:

1.

Credit of Service Tax: The same must be properly reflected in the last service tax returns and documentation must be in place to establish the same as per Section 140(1).

2.

Credit of Excise Duty/ CVD/SAD: Since, currently builders are not availing the credit of excise duty & CVD. GST on ongoing project/contracts

Construction projects normally last for 3-4 years which is generally categorized as "continuous supply of service" in service tax as well as under GST. In transitory phase of GST, many projects are half-finished from their completion stage which creates lot of ambiguity in minds of businesses and professionals that whether such incomplete projects are liable under service tax/VAT or under GST.

As per section 142(11)(c) of CGST Act, 2017, where both VAT and Service Tax has been paid on any supplies which are to be made under the GST regime, GST shall be payable on the said supplies under GST Act and the person shall be entitled to take credit of VAT or Service Tax paid under the existing law to the extent of the said supplies made in the GST regime.

This provisions specifically provides that if any activity done by a builder is covered under the scope of supply under GST, then GST is payable on invoices issued after 1st July, 2017 and if any service tax and VAT is paid, then amount of tax paid earlier is eligible as credit for payment of GST.

Therefore, it can be seen that on all the advances received by developers in present regime for which supply have to be made in GST regime, GST will be applicable and it would a compliance burden to match invoices with the advances received earlier and their tax treatment.

Other Critical issues and implication of GST on such issues

1.

Valuation of Works contract: Currently, developers have to bifurcate the service of works contract in to "original works" or "other than original works" in Service Tax Law for different valuation provisions. Further, different classifications were also given in different state VAT Laws. In GST, whole service of works contract is deemed as a pure service as per Schedule II of CGST Act, 2017 and accordingly rate of 18% will be leviable on whole amount ending earlier litigation.

2.

Reverse Charge Mechanism: Currently, under reverse charge mechanism in Service Tax, developers have to pay tax as service receiver in respect of many services. Majority of the services on which developers have to pay significant tax in Service Tax are works contract services, manpower or security services, rent-a-cab etc. Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM) have been continued in GST regime as well, but these services which constituted major portion of tax payments for developers are not covered under RCM in GST and therefore will provide a major relief to Real estate sector.

However, a new concept of reverse charge is introduced in GST in which, every registered person have to pay tax under reverse charge on supplies received from unregistered person. Thus, developers have to pay tax under RCM on all purchases from unregistered person. It might have significant impact in case any developers has significant availment of services from unregistered sub - contractors as amount of such transaction is also very high.

The courts generally held that the phrase 'public carriage of passengers or goods' cannot be construed in such manner as to exclude from the ambit of 'railways' the sidings built and owned by organizations other than the government. [Para 6] Article 366(20) of the Constitution excludes from the ambit of 'railway' only (a) a tramway wholly within a municipal area and (b) any line of communication wholly situate in one State and declared by Parliament by law not to be a railway. The Parliament excludes by law, apart from the tramways, the lines of rails mentioned under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989, being rails built solely for the purpose of recreation. The term 'public carriage', therefore, cannot be given any meaning that may add more exclusion than specifically provided under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989. DVC - a public sector undertaking - is the owner of the railway siding being built. It is meant for carriage of coal and oil fuel to RTPS. The purpose of the carriage of goods is, therefore, not recreation, but producing public goods like electricity. It is, therefore, not excluded under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989. The construction of the private siding that the applicant refers to, therefore, pertains to 'railways'. From the definition, a work shall be treated as Works Contract if that work is done for land or earth or for immovable property and there is transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such contract. Immovable property cannot be moved. It cannot be separated from the land or earth. If it is detached it shall have to destroy. In the case at hand, the 'Employer's Requirements, Particular Specifications-4B Telecommunication General Specification' - gives the outline summary of the various systems and sub-systems which are applicable to the Telecommunication scope and the outline description of the works said to be the works of the applicant. On going through same, it is observed that the work involves installation of the individual systems at platforms, stations, other select locations along the corridor and is integrated at the Operation Control Corridor (OCC) at Koyambedu and the Telecommunications Infrastructure implementation is to be synchronized with the civil construction phases. Further the scope of works of the applicant like Public Address and Voice Alarm System, CCTV System, Passenger Information Display System, Office Telephone System, etc. requires installation on specific locations, namely ceiling and the like and these goods once installed, may not necessarily be damaged while removing. The applicant has not established with documents that the works contracted to them are to be executed on immovable property as required under definition of 'Works Contract' given above. The applicant has stated that in the Pre-GST regime, under Service Tax, the applicant being a supplier of Works Contract Service relating to infrastructure project of railways, in capacity of sub-contractor was exempted from service tax and had claimed the benefit of entry 3(v) of Notification 11/2017 - C.T. (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as above. The definition of 'Works Contract' as it existed in the 'Service Tax' law is different from that defined under section 2(119) of GST Act. Under GST, only those defined works carried out on any immovable property is covered under 'Works Contract'. Thus without documentary proof of the works contracted/undertaken like related diagrams/plans/schedules/Pictures/detailed write-up on the works, etc. in the absence of submission of the entire sub-contract agreement, it is not possible for this Authority to conclude that the works are done on the immovable property and once installed, the goods/equipments cannot be dismantled without damage so as to hold that the work undertaken is 'Works Contract' as per section 2(119) of the Act. As the applicant has stated that it will not be possible for them to furnish the entire sub-contract agreement which contains the requisite details, in the absence of the documentation works could not be said as 'Works Contract' as per section 2(119). [Para 11.3]

The other criteria to be satisfied are the supply should be by way of 'construction, erection, commissioning or installation of original works' pertaining to railways, including monorail and metro. Original work is defined in Para 2(zs) of the Notification No. 12/2017 - C.T. (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

From the submissions, it is seen that the work of the applicant includes Installation of the various systems on designing, manufacture and supply and therefore is 'Original work' as defined in the notification.

The work of the applicant is on the lines, stations and locations of land appurtenant and, therefore, this criterion is satisfied. [Para 11.4]

To summarize, the entry at 3(v) do not specify the class of service provider to whom it applies. The entry is specific to the composite supply of works contract pertaining to railways including monorail and metro. This view is fortified by the justification of the recommendation of the Fitment Committee to the 25th GST Council meeting (available in Volume-2 of the Agenda) after which the downward revision of the rate was effected.

Andhra Pradesh State Financial Corporation (APSFC) is a term lending institution established in 1956 for promoting small and medium scale industries in Andhra Pradesh under the provisions of the State Financial Corporation Act, 1951. The functions of the corporation are to launch entrepreneur friendly schemes to provide term loans, working capital term loans, special and seed capital assistance, etc.

The APSFC is established by the Government and the Government of Andhra Pradesh is having more than 90 per cent of control over it. Thus it is covered under the definition of 'Government Entity'. Therefore, the APSFC is a 'Government Entity' for the purpose of GST matters.

The applicant agreed for construction of office building to APSFC, which includes procurement and supply of goods and services for agreed consideration. The activity of construction includes both supply of goods and also services.

Section 2(119) defines 'works contract' as a contract for building, construction, fabrication, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, maintenance, renovation, alternation or commissioning of any immovable property wherein transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) is involved in the execution of such contract.

The composite supply of works contract under section 2(119) is treated as supply of service in terms of Serial No. 6(a) of Schedule II of the CGST Act.

The Government of India vide Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 notified the rate of GST applicable on supply of services. Under this Notification for Heading No. 9954, the applicable rate of GST is 9 per cent.

Vide Notification No. 24/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 21-9-2017, Government of India by inserting entry (vi) notified concessional GST rate of 6 per cent for the construction services provided to Central Government, State Government, Union Territory, a local authority or a Governmental Authority by way of construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion, fitting out, repair, maintenance, renovation, or alteration of —

(c)

a residential complex predominantly meant for self-use or the use of their employees or other persons specified in paragraph 3 of the Schedule III of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017.

The applicant is engaged in construction work of office building for APSFC, which is meant for governance of corporation activities. The applicant is of the view that the use of the said construction (building) is not for any business or so.

As seen from the Annual Reports for the years 2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18 as made available by APSFC in its website, it is engaged in providing financial services to industries and entrepreneurs. The income it is getting is from interest on loans and advances and also service charges, upfront fee/commitment fee, sale of application forms, profit on sale of assets, commission on insurance, rent received, etc. Therefore, the activities of APSFC are business activities and not otherwise. Service tax on works contract

SUDHIR HALAKHANDI*

The Finance Minister with a sole motto, ‘when transfer of property involved in works contract is taxable, then why the transfer of services involved in works contract is not taxable’ proposed one more complicated levy of service tax on works contract vide the Finance Bill, 2007. Now the contractors involved in works contract will have to pay service tax on transfer of services. This write-up highlights the types of contract where the levy is attracted, where the levy is not attracted and the composition scheme while making reference to departmental clarification in this regard. The rules of valuation and the composition scheme will be declared later though anticipating the requirement of opting for composition scheme, the law-makers have already disclosed the rate of composition as 2 per cent on the whole amount of contract.

Introduction

1. Transfer of property in goods involved in works contract is taxable under the State tax i.e. VAT or sales tax. This levy under the State sales tax laws was a very complicated levy and the complications further increased on the introduction of VAT. Most of the contractors have opted for composition schemes introduced by the State Governments. The service tax was introduced in 1994 with a sole motto ‘When goods are taxable why not services’. On the same ground the Finance Minister seems to have a thought that ‘When transfer of property involved in works contract is taxable, then why the transfer of services involved in works contract is not taxable’ and, hence, he proposed one more complicated levy of service tax on works contract. Now the contractors involved in execution of works contract will have to pay service tax on transfer of services also. The rules of valuation and the composition scheme in this regard will be declared later though, anticipating the requirement of opting for composition scheme, the law makers have already disclosed the rate of composition as 2 per cent on the whole amount of contract.

Finance Minister’s speech

2. The relevant portion of the Finance Minister’s Speech is as under :

"154. State Governments levy a tax on the transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of a works contract. The value of services in a works contract should attract service tax. Hence, I propose to levy of service tax on services involved in the execution of a works contract. However, I also propose an optional composition scheme under which service tax will be levied at only 2 per cent of the total value of the works contract."

Service tax on works contract

3. The levy of service tax and its taxability is defined and explained in section 65(105)(zzzza ), which is proposed to be added to the Finance Act, 1994 by the Finance Bill, 2007.

This section reads as under :

"Taxable service means a service provided or to be provided :

to any person, by any other person in relation to the execution of a works contract, excluding works contract in respect of roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams.

Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-clause, ‘works contract’ means a contract wherein,—

(i )Transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such contract is leviable to tax as sale of goods, and

(ii )Such contract is for the purposes of carrying out,—

( a)Erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery, equipment or structures, whether pre-fabricated or otherwise, installation of electrical and electronic devices, plumbing, drain laying or other installations for transport of fluids, heating, ventilation or air-conditioning including related pipe work, duct work and sheet metal work, thermal insulation, sound insulation, fire proofing or water proofing, lift and escalator, fire escape staircases or elevators; or

( b)Construction of a new building or a civil structure or a part thereof, or of a pipeline or conduit, primarily for the purposes of commerce or industry; or

( c)Construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

( d)Completion and finishing services, repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services, in relation to (b) and (c); or

( e)Turnkey projects including Engineering Procurement and Construction or Commissioning (EPC) projects;,

Real Estate Services relating to residential and commercial apartments

23.1 Background

Taxation of real estate sector has always been problematic issue. The major reason is that the sector is still unorganized. The complications started after introduction of State tax on works contract. The problem aggravated after introduction of service tax on works contract.

The State tax and Service tax was merged on introduction of GST w.e.f. 1-7-2017. However, many issues were still unresolved.

Hence, the GST structure on real estate services relating to residential and commercial apartments has been thoroughly altered w.e.f. 1-4-2019.

This service falls under service code 9954.

The highlights of revised scheme are as follows -

The revised scheme applies to residential and commercial apartments which are covered under RERA [Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016].

The provisions do not apply to construction of single houses or works contracts not covered under RERA.

The new scheme is compulsory for projects commenced on or after 1-4-2019. In respect of ongoing projects as on 31-3-2019, the promoter has option to shift to new scheme w.e.f. 1-4-2019 (without ITC) or continue under earlier scheme (with ITC)

Under new scheme, the GST rates for residential apartments are as follows - (a) CGST 0.5% plus SGST/UTGST 0.5% (total 1%) or IGST 1% (without ITC) for affordable residential apartments (b) CGST 2.5% plus SGST/UTGST 2.5% (total 5%) or IGST 5% (without ITC) for other residential apartments, where price includes value of land.

In respect of commercial apartments (shops, offices, godowns etc.) in RREP, the GST rate is CGST 2.5% plus SGST/UTGST 2.5% (total 5%) or IGST 5% (without ITC). In respect of construction of commercial apartments (other than RREP), the GST rate is CGST 6% plus SGST/UTGST 6% (total 12%) or IGST 12% (with ITC).

In case of ongoing projects, if the promoter intends to shift to new scheme (of 1%/5%) w.e.f. 1-4-2019, he is required to refund excess ITC availed as on 31-3-2019 or get credit of ITC less claimed as on 31-3-2019.

RREP (Residential Real Estate Project) means Real Estate Project (REP) of residential apartments with commercial apartments not more than 15% of total carpet area of REP.

23.1-8 Redevelopment is subject to GST

Generally in re-development project, land is owned by a society, comprising members of the society with each member entitled to his share by way of an apartment. When it becomes necessary after the lapse of a certain period, society or its flat owners may engage a promoter (builder/developer) for undertaking re-construction. Society/individual apartment owners give 'No Objection Certificate' (NOC) or permission to the promoter (builder/developer), for re-construction. The promoter (builder/developer) constructs apartments with same or different carpet area for original owners of apartment and additionally may also be involved in one or more of the following: (i) construct some additional apartments for sale to others (ii) arrange for rental accommodation or rent payments for society members/original owners for stay during the period of re-construction (iii) pay an additional amount to the original owners of flats in the society.

Under this model, the promoter (builder/developer) receives consideration for the construction service provided by him, from two categories of service receivers. First category is the society/members of the society, who transfer development rights over the land (including the permission for additional number of apartments), to the promoter (builder/developer). The second category of service receivers consist of buyers of apartments other than the society/members. Generally, they pay by cash.

In both the cases, GST is payable as in first case, the promoter receives consideration in form of TDR and in other cases, by cash.

Gannon Dunkerley & Co. v. State of Rajasthan (1993) 66 Taxman 229 = 1993 AIR SCW 2621 = (1993) 1 SCC 364 = (1993) 88 STC 204 (SC 5 member Constitution bench) is another important judgment on 'Works Contract'. Here, it was held that taxable event is the transfer of property in the goods involved in the execution of a works contract. The said transfer of property takes place when goods are incorporated in the works. Hence, value of goods at the time of incorporation in the works can constitute measure for levy of tax. However, cost of incorporation of the goods in works contract cannot be made part of measure for the levy of tax. It was held that value of goods involved in works contract would have to be considered for taxation on works contract. Charges for labour and services have to be deducted from total value of works contract. - - Profits relatable to supply of material can be included in value of goods and profits which are relatable to supply of labour and services are to be excluded.

In aforesaid judgment, it was held that value of goods involved in the execution of a works contract will have to be determined by taking into account the value of entire works contract and deducting therefrom the charges towards labour and services, which cover - (a) Labour charges for execution of the works (b) Amount paid to a sub-contractor for labour and services (c) Charges for planning, designing and architect's fees (d) Charges for obtaining on hire or otherwise machinery and tools used for the execution of works contract (e) Cost of consumables such as water, electricity, fuel etc., used in the execution of works contract, the property in which is not transferred in the course of execution of a works contract (f) Cost of establishment of the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services (g) Other similar expenses relatable to supply of labour and services (h) Profit earned by the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services.

The amounts deductible under these heads will have to be determined in the light of the facts of a particular case, on the basis of the material produced by the contractor.

Moreover, tax cannot be levied on goods which are taxable under sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST Act and goods covered under sections 14 and 15 of CST Act. If contractor is not able to give detailed break up, legislature can prescribe scales for deductions permissible on account of cost of labour and services for various types of works contract.

It is permissible to have a uniform rate for works contract. This rate may be different from the rates applicable to individual goods.

The judgment in this case was subsequently followed in Builders' Association of India v. State of Karnataka (1993) 88 STC 248 = AIR 1993 SC 991 = (1993) 1 SCC 409 = 1993 AIR SCW 152 (SC - 5 member bench).

In Daelim Industrial Co. v. State of Assam (2003) 130 STC 53 (Gau HC), it was held that in case of works contract, tax is payable only of value of goods and not on cost of design and engineering.

uThere must be transfer of property in goods.

uIt must be a turnkey project

2.2 Rule 3 - New Set of Rules named as ‘The Works Contract (Composition Scheme for Payment of Service Tax) Rules, 2007’ is inserted by Notification No. 32/2007-Service Tax, dated May 22, 2007. Rule 3 of said Rules reads as under—

"3.(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in section 67 of the Act and rule 2A of the Service (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, the person liable to pay service tax in relation to works contract service shall have the option to discharge his service tax liability on the works contract service provided or to be provided, instead of paying service tax at the rate specified in section 66 of the Act, by paying an amount equivalent to two per cent of the gross amount charged for the works contract.

Explanation.—For the purposes of this rule, gross amount charged for the works contract shall not include Value Added Tax (VAT) or sales tax, as the case may be, paid on transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the said works contract.

(2) The provider of taxable service shall not take CENVAT credit of duties or cess paid on any inputs, used in or in relation to the said works contract under the provisions of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

(3) The provider of taxable service who opts to pay service tax under these rules shall exercise such option in respect of a works contract prior to payment of service tax in respect of the said works contract and the option so exercised shall be applicable for the entire works contract and shall not be withdrawn until the completion of the said works contract."

As I understand, there is 1% Vat in Maharashtra and 0.6% in Gujarat.

In AP VAT the builders have a special option of paying VAT @ 1.25% (Other options are also available).

Vat is payable by builders in Karnataka and Rajasthan for which various scheme are available. Vat is payable in Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal also.

In MP, it seems, the transaction is treated as deemed sale of goods and taxed by excluding value of land. In Haryana, as I understand, builders are not liable to pay State Vat but they have to deduct tax (TDS) and pay to Government. Really, TDS does not mean that Vat is payable by the builder.

It seems in Delhi, department is of the view that Vat is payable but builders are not agreeing on basis of Raheja's case. In any case, they are liable to deduction tax at source on works contract. However, TDS does not mean they are paying State Vat on the works contract.

Thus, in States where the builders/developers are not liable to pay Vat, their service will have to be classified as 'construction' service and not 'works contract' service. The effect would be that they are not entitled to pay service tax under composition scheme of 40%/60%.

However, they can avail 25%/30% abatement scheme if the value includes value of land.

Builders can pay service tax on value of services - Even where builder finds that 25% scheme is not suitable, it does not mean that they have to pay service tax on entire value of works contract. Service tax would still be payable only on value of services. However, in many construction contracts, finding value of service is not easy. In my view, they can still follow the principles of composition scheme, though legally they are not entitled to that scheme.

Builders/Developers liable to pay Vat on construction of residential flats/commercial shops if State law provides - If State Vat Act provides, builders/developers will be liable to pay Vat on construction of residential flats/commercial shops. The issue is discussed in next chapter.

16.2-1 Exemption to sub-contractor providing works contract service to other contractor

Following service is exempt - Sub-contractor providing services by way of works contract to another contractor providing works contract services which are exempt - clause 29(h) Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012.

Thus, if main works contract is exempt, sub-contractor providing works contract service to main contractor will be exempt from service tax. This exemption is only when the sub-contractor provides works contract service and not in other cases.

16.2-2 Sub-contractor liable even if main contractor pays service tax

CBE&C vide circular No. 999.03/23.8.07 has clarified that a sub-contractor is also a taxable service provider. His services are taxable even if these are used by main provider for completion of his work. The sub-contractor is liable even if the service is input service of the main contractor.

Sub-contractor is liable even if main contractor is exempt from service tax - CBE&C circular No. 138/7/2011-ST dated 6-5-2011.

Sub-contractor is liable even if main contractor has paid service tax - Engineers India Technical Services v. CCE (2014) 73 VST 206 (CESTAT).

In Sew Construction Ltd. v. CCE (2011) 32 STT 120 = 12 taxmann.com 12 (CESTAT), it has been held that sub-contractor was liable even prior to 23-8-2007.

However, if sub-contractor is providing a service which is exempt, then he will not be liable e.g. if a contractor is providing works contract service which is exempt and if he entrusts that work to sub-contractor, then the sub-contractor will be providing the works contract service (which is exempt) and hence he will also not be liable to pay service tax. However, if the sub-contractor provides some other service like consultancy, cargo handling, clearing and forwarding which is taxable, then the sub-contractor will be liable to service tax even if the main contractor is exempt - CBE&C circular No. 147/16/2011-ST dated 21-10-2011 (The circular is with reference to works contract service but is applicable to all services provided by sub-contractors).

INTEREST ON CREDIT CARD OUTSTANDINGS NOT LIABLE TO SERVICE TAX

5. I am a user of credit cards. I use the same for payment of my utility bills, purchases, etc. Often, on account of one reason or the another, I delay in payment of the credit card outstandings and interest is charged for such delay (generally, no interest is charged when payment is made within due date, but some ancillary charges are debited). While going through my credit card bills, I find that the bank has charged service tax even on the interest amount. I understand that credit card management services may be liable to service tax, but, there can't be any charge of service tax on interest amount. Please clarify.

Interest on loans is excluded from charge of service tax by virtue of negative list entry under section 66D(n) of the Finance Act, 1994. As per section 65B(30), interest means interest payable in any manner in respect of any moneys borrowed or debt incurred (including a deposit, claim or other similar right or obligation).

Interest for delayed payment of consideration of services is excluded from value by virtue of Rule 6(2) of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006.

In this regard, the Guidance Note, dated 20-6-2012 has clarified that charges for late payment of dues on credit card outstandings are not excludible from taxable value for the following reasons :

(i)

No exclusion under Rule 6(2) of Valuation Rules : Interest for delayed payment of any consideration for the sale of goods or provision of service has been specifically excluded from value by Rule 6 of the Valuation Rules. However, in the case of credit cards the credit extended is not for the delayed payment of consideration for the provision of services. The services in the case of the credit card are by way of levy of issuing charges or the commission charged from merchants, etc. The interest is not for the consideration for the use of the card. Thus, exclusion under valuation rules will not be available.

(ii)

No exclusion under the negative list : Such credit extended will also not amount to loans or advances. Loans and advances are meant to signify amounts contractually negotiated as such (loan or advance) and not merely a failure to pay an amount at the due date. The exorbitant charges have also no relationship with the prevailing interest rate for the same class of creditworthiness and are in the nature of consideration for the services rendered for using the convenience of using the services by way of a credit card and, hence, are taxable.

In a prima facie view expressed by the Tribunal in Canara Bank v. CCE&C (LTU), [2013] 29 taxmann.com 157 (Bang. - CESTAT), it was held that interest on credit card dues partakes character of 'interest on loan' and, therefore, it shall not form part of value of credit card related services.

The said prima facie view appears to be correct view, as 'interest' will fall under section 66D(n), even if rate is exorbitant. The view of the Department appears to be more based on economic sense rather than legal interpretation. The same doesn't appear to be correct.

Accordingly, as far as charge of interest by bank is concerned, you may bring this to the notice of the bank. If the bank refuses to accept this view (which is likely, so as to avoid any conflict and further, because burden is transferred to clients), you may seek action against the Bank or file a claim for refund of service tax paid by you under section 83 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

It is also seen that the subject contract does not satisfy the descriptions mentioned in clauses (i) to (xii) except clause (ii) of section 5 of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended.

The subject work to be undertaken by the applicant is a composite supply of works contract, since it includes supply of both, goods and services and does not fall in any of the clauses (i) to (xii) except clause (ii) of section 5 of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended. Hence, the subject contract is taxable and the tax rate to be applied is 18 percent GST. [Para 5]

Thus, the supply of goods or services for 'setting up of network' would qualify as a Composite supply of works contract as defined in clause (119) of section 2 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017.

The rate of tax applicable to the supplies will be 18 per cent GST. [Para 6]

Coverage of 'works contract' under service tax

For purpose of service tax, the term 'works contract' has been defined as follows—

'"Works contract" means a contract wherein transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such contract is leviable to tax as sale of goods and such contract is for the purpose of carrying out construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion, fitting out, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration of any movable or immovable property or for carrying out any other similar activity or a part thereof in relation to such property - section 65B(54) of Finance Act, 1994 as introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012.'

Coverage of services under works contract service - Though the definition of works contract under service tax and CST/State Vat Acts are quite different, practically most of the works contracts taxable under State Vat laws will get covered under service tax also. This is because definition of 'works contract' under service tax covers wide range of activities relating to both movable and immovable property.

This view has also been expressed in para 6.8.6 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

Thus, following will get covered under this definition :

(a)

Erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery, equipment or structures

(b)

Construction of buildings and civil structures

(c)

turnkey projects

(d)

maintenance services relating to goods where goods and service both are involved as composite contract (e.g. Annual Maintenance Contracts)

(e)

Job work (which does not amount to manufacture) where job worker uses some of his own material (which may be even minor) [Job work will get covered under the term 'alteration']

Departmental clarification - Laying of pipeline or conduit, erection, commissioning of machinery, equipment and structures, painting of building, renovation of building, flooring, repairs of building would be covered under 'works contract' - Paras 5.8.2 to 5.8.6 of Annexure A of MF(DR) TRU DO F. No. 334/1/2012-TRU dated 16-3-2012.

The circular stated that works contract will not cover 'tailoring or development of photograph'. However, in view of revised definition of 'works contract' under service tax law w.e.f. 1-7-2012, even tailoring or development of photograph will come under 'works contract' service.

State Vat/CST should be payable - One basic requirement is that the activity should be subject to tax as sale of goods. (The activity may be relating to movable or immovable property)

Laying of pipeline is not erection and commissioning service - Pipeline is not a plant, machinery, equipment or structure. The activity is not taxable as erection, installation and commissioning service - CCE v. Surindra Engineering (2015) 79 VST 436 (CESTAT).

In Indian Hume Pipe Co. Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 16 STT 136 = 26 VST 63 (CESTAT), assessee was manufacturing and supplying pre-stressed concrete pipes for water supply. He also undertook contract for construction of pipeline by excavation, conveying and lowering pipes and joining material, laying to proper grade and alignment, refilling trenches, construction of air valves. It was held that this is not installation and commissioning service. In case of laying of pipeline, appellant were not undertaking activity of erection of pipeline. The appellant did not set up a pipeline but constructed one. Long distance pipeline is not a 'plant'. - followed in Lalit Constructions v. CCE (2012) 37 STT 687 = 27 taxmann.com 194 (CESTAT).

In Strategic Engineering v. ACCE (2012) 49 VST 381 (Mad HC), it was held that laying of pipes for transportation of fluid is not erection, commissioning service.

10.8-1 Tax can be only on value of material

Builders Association of India v. UOI (1989) 2 SCR 320 = 73 STC 370 = (1989) 2 SCC 645 = AIR 1989 SC 1371 (SC 5 member Constitution bench) is a landmark judgment of Supreme Court on 'works contract'. The background of this case is that after amendment to Constitution in 1983, various State Governments imposed levy on works contract. The tax was levied by some State Governments on full value of contract which included the material cost and other costs like labour, supply of services etc.

However, in the judgment, Hon. Supreme Court held that the power of States to levy tax on works contract is subject to limitation of Article 286 i.e. tax cannot be levied by State on (a) outside the State (b) during import/export. (c) Restrictions placed on 'declared goods' are applicable even while levying tax on works contract. Further, tax cannot be imposed on full value of contract. The tax is on 'transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract.' Thus, tax on works contract can be levied only on 'value of goods involved' and not on whole value of works contract.

In State of Jharkhand v. Voltas Ltd. (2007) 7 STR 106 = 7 VST 317 (SC) also it was confirmed that sales tax can be levied only on value of goods. All charges/amounts are deductible from value of works contract except value of goods sold in execution of works contract, for computing taxable value.

In Imagic Creative Pvt. Ltd. v. CCT (2008) 2 SCC 614 = 12 STT 392 = 12 VST 371 = 9 STR 337 (SC), it has been held that service tax and Vat (sales tax) are mutually exclusive. In case of a composite contract, Vat cannot be imposed on portion relating to value of service.

Restrictions applicable to declared goods apply to declared goods used in works contract - Provisions relating to declared goods are applicable even if the declared goods are used in works contract. Thus, Vat rate cannot be more than that applicable to declared goods - Smt B Narasamma v. DCCT (2016) 96 VST 357 (SC).

CST Act imposes restrictions on State Government in levying tax on declared goods. These restrictions apply to goods involved in works contract also - Afcons Infrastructure Ltd. v. State of Assam (2007) 9 VST 195 (Gau HC).

Vat/sales tax is payable on iron and steel used in works contract at rate applicable to declared goods - URC Construction Ltd. v. DCCT (2008) 11 VST 896 (Karn HC) - view confirmed in Smt B Narasamma v. DCTO (2016) 57 GST 39 = 72 taxmann.com 349 = 96 VST 357 (SC).

What was covered

Industrial and commercial construction and construction of residential complex having more than 12 residential units (flats/houses) was taxable.

Repairs, alteration, renovation of existing building is also subject to tax.

Approved plan and municipal regulations to determine whether building is for commerce or industry.

Post construction stand alone services relating to completion or finishing are taxable.

Sub-contractors providing the construction services (to main contractor or to any other person) will be liable to service tax.

Repairs of roads was not taxable.

What was not covered?

Services provided in respect of roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams.

Construction of educational, religious, Government buildings etc. not taxable, as it is not commercial or industrial construction.

Residential complex which is constructed by a person directly engaging any other person for designing or planning of the layout, and the construction of such complex is intended for personal use as residence by such person - "personal use" includes permitting the complex for use as residence by another person on rent or without consideration.

Construction by builder or developer for personal use of customer (even if it is in residential complex).

Construction of one house in residential complex is not taxable if direct contract given by individual for residential purposes to builder or developer.

Construction of single house or residential complex with 12 or less than 12 residential units is not taxable.

Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers had released Draft of model GST Act and IGST Act on 14-6-2016. Later draft rules relating to registration, invoice, payments, returns and refunds were released in September, 2016 by CBE&C. FAQs were also released by CBE&C in September, 2016.

On basis of various suggestions received, fresh model laws have been released by GST Council Secretariat on 26-11-2016. Following three drafts have been released—

1.

Model GST Law

2.

Model IGST Law

3.

Draft Goods and Service Tax (Compensation to the States for Loss of Revenue) Bill, 2016

Many changes have been made compared to earlier draft. It is heartening to note that many suggestions from trade and industry have been considered and suitable changes have been made.

These drafts have already been discussed at officers' level. Now, these will be placed before GST Council which is scheduled to meet on 2-12-2016. Finishing touches may be given in the meeting.

After approval of GST Council, the Bill will be presented before Parliament in week commencing on 5-12-2016.

If all goes well, the Bills may be passed in winter 2016 session of Parliament and the GST will see light of day on 1-4-2017. Of course there are many slips between cup and the lip.

Detailed write up is attached. The highlights of major changes vis-à-vis Model Laws released in June, 2016 are given below.

Ceiling on GST Rates

The new Model Law specifies ceiling on GST rates as follows - SGST - 14%, CGST - 14% and IGST - 28%.

Of course, this ceiling is illusory as section 8 of GST (Compensation to the States for Loss of Revenue) Bill, 2016 makes provision for levy and collection of GST Compensation Cess on supplies of goods and services. This cess will be non-vatable.

Thus, all what is achieved by GST can be lost through such cess. Only solace is that this cess can be levied by Central Government and not individual State Governments.

Definition of 'supply without consideration' pruned and made more practical

The earlier definition of 'supply without consideration' as contained in Schedule I was very broad. It covered transactions which were for private use. This would have created huge amount of litigation, particularly because as per provisions of input tax credit, input credit of expenses not related to business was anyway not available. Thus, this would have created double whammy.

The revised definition of 'supply without consideration' in Schedule I is as follows—

1.

Permanent transfer/disposal of business assets where input tax credit has been availed on such assets.

2.

Supply of goods or services between related persons, or between distinct persons as specified in section 10, when made in the course or furtherance of business.

3.

Supply of goods—

(a)

by a principal to his agent where the agent undertakes to supply such goods on behalf of the principal, or

(b)

by an agent to his principal where the agent undertakes to receive such goods on behalf of the principal.

4.

Importation of services by a taxable person from a related person or from any of his other establishments outside India, in the course or furtherance of business.

The transactions between agent and principal will be subject to GST on goods only when Agent receives the goods (like C&F Agency or Consignment Agent). If the Agent is commission agent and does not receive goods, he will be liable only to GST on his commission.

Definition of 'works contract' restricted to services relating to immovable property

The earlier model law was covering works contracts of 'movable property' also. Now, only works contracts relating to immovable property will alone be covered (though first part of definition of 'works contract' still contains the words 'transfer of property in goods is involved in the execution of such contract', which are likely to cause confusion and litigation).

The revised definition as per section 2(110) of new Model Law is as follows—

"works contract" means a contract wherein transfer of property in goods is involved in the execution of such contract and includes contract for building, construction, fabrication, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration or commissioning of any immovable property.
